rows.description: A person worried about a parent's health or a project's outcome does what is possible and releases the rest. Separating what is in one's hands from what is not reduces suffering.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Confusing letting go with giving up [Observer]
rows.description: A friend hears someone say I have let go while still hurting and avoiding the topic. Real letting go is quiet and peaceful, whereas avoidance is tense and easily triggered.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22
related mind states: confusion, calm, hurt

rows.description: A toddler babbles, pauses and waits for the parent to reply, then babbles again. Serve-and-return exchanges are the base of all later conversation.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A child bursts into the middle of an adult's talk because the thought might vanish. Waiting is hard, and a hand signal or a promise of a turn helps more than scolding.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A group of friends notices one person who always takes the floor and rarely asks anything back. Others start disengaging quietly, and the dominant one often does not notice.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A young adult in a group asks a quiet friend what they think, opening a turn without pressure. Sharing the floor makes conversations fairer and richer.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A young employee notices that in a meeting seniors talk in long stretches while juniors wait for gaps that never come. Naming a gap or asking a chair for a minute is a skill that can be learned.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A child hears a parent's instruction while looking at a toy and does not process it. Getting eye level and a name call before speaking helps attention.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A child hears only enough to defend themselves or correct. Most everyday listening stays at this surface level.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager tells a friend a worry and notices the friend puts the phone down and asks a follow-up. That one act tells the teenager they matter more than any advice.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
